list.listitem: The majority of asymptomatic patients with hypercalcemia have primary hyperparathyroidism.C

Many patients with mild primary hyperparathyroidism remain stable without surgery, but long-term monitoring is required because hypercalcemia, kidney disease, nephrolithiasis, or skeletal complications may progress.B

Treat hypercalcemia of malignancy with IV hydration and either denosumab or an IV bisphosphonate. Denosumab is conditionally preferred, particularly in patients with significant renal impairment or recurrent/refractory hypercalcemia.B
Initial treatment of symptomatic or severe hypercalcemia is intravenous isotonic fluids plus denosumab or an IV bisphosphonate when indicated..C

For patients with moderate acute or symptomatic hypercalcemia of malignancy (HCM), IV hydration with isotonic saline (with the rate individulized to the patients volume status, renal and cardiac function and urine ouitput) and denosumab are recommended. In severe HCM IV hydration, calcitonin and IV bisphophonates or denosumab.B
Parathyroidectomy is definitive treatment. Evidence that surgery consistently improves nonspecific neurocognitive symptoms or quality of life in otherwise asymptomatic patients is inconclusive.B

background.definition: Hypercalcemia occurs when the serum calcium exceeds normal limits. The typical upper limit of normal is 10.5 mg/dL, but the ionized calcium is a more accurate measure and is typically 4.0 to 5.6 mg/dL (1.0-1.4 mmol/L). Mild hypercalcemia is 10.5 to 12.5 mg/dL; moderate hypercalcemia is 12.5 to 14 mg/dL; severe hypercalcemia is >14 mg/dL.

list.listitem: 0.2 to 0.5 per 1000 new cases per year in general U.S. population.
Hypercalcemia reported in 7.5% of patients seen in the emergency department.
Occurs in 5% to 10% of advanced malignancies.
Primary hyperparathyroidism and malignancy are the cause in approximately 90% of patients.
Hyperparathyroidism (primary, secondary, or tertiary).
Malignancy (any bony metastasis, also myeloma, lymphoma, paraneoplastic syndromes).
Medications (thiazides, lithium, SGLT-2 inhibitors but evidence is limited and the association is uncommon, immune checkpoint inhibitors).
Excess bone turnover (immobilization, Paget's disease).
Genetic disorders (familial hypocalciuric hypercalcemia).
Granulomatous disease, including sarcoidosis.
Vitamin D or A intoxication; use of vitamin D analogues such as eldecalcitol.
Milk-alkali syndrome (calcium carbonate ingestion).
Thyrotoxicosis.
Hodgkin lymphoma
Adrenal insufficiency
Ketogenic diet in children

Parathyroid hormone (PTH) raises serum calcium by increasing renal calcium reabsorption, stimulating bone resorption, and increasing renal production of calcitriol, which indirectly increases intestinal calcium absorption.
Malignancy may involve osteolytic activity (e.g., breast cancer) or PTH-like humoral activity (e.g., squamous cell carcinoma).
Granulomatous diseases increase activity of 1-alpha hydroxylase, thereby leading to increased (1,25-OH) vitamin D.
Secondary osteoporosis in primary hyperparathyroidism is accelerated in cortical bone (radius), but cancellous bone (lumbar spine) is well preserved.

Serum PTH level important for identifying potential cause ().C
Primary hyperparathyroidism and malignancy account for more than 80% of cases of hypercalcemia.C

Differential.Differential_Features: Elevated intact PTH in relation to serum calcium
Evidence of malignancy, particularly bony metastases
Abnormal bone x-rays and biochemical markers of bone turnover
Granulomatous disease (sarcoid, berylliosis, tuberculosis) found on chest x-ray
Elevated PTH, but low urinary calcium
Thiazide, lithium use, excessive intake of vitamin A or D
History, predisposing condition with high bone turnover

list.listitem: Patients most often present asymptomatically following finding of elevated serum calcium on routine laboratory testing.

Symptoms are nonspecific and may include polyuria, polydipsia, constipation, nausea, cognitive changes, weakness, and fatigue; symptoms become more likely as calcium rises rapidly or exceeds approximately 12 mg/dL.
When patient presents with elevated serum calcium (>10.4 or 2.6 mmol/L), either repeat to confirm or confirm with ionized calcium (usual range 4.0-5.6 mg/dL or 1.0-1.4 mmol/L).
Unadjusted total calcium correlated with ionized calcium at least as well as albumin-adjusted formulas and produced fewer classification errors, particularly in patients with hypoalbuminemia.

Therefore, conform unexpected hypercalcemia with repeat total calcium. Measure ionized calcium when albumin is substantially abnormal, the result is discordant with the clinical picture, or accurate classification is important; albumin-correction formulas may misclassify calcium status.
Intact serum PTH is the recommended test to diagnose primary hyperparathyroidism.
See algorithm in for an approach to evaluation.
A clinical decision rule can help identify those patients with an increased risk of malignancy.
Key factors include serum albumin, phosphate, chloride, gamma glutamyl transferase, and excreted calcium.
See algorithm in for a suggested approach to evaluation.

Initial treatment of symptomatic or severe hypercalcemia is intravenous hydration and denosumab or an IV bisphosphonate.C For patients with moderate acute or symptomatic hypercalcemia of malignancy (HCM), IV hydration and denosumab are recommended. In severe HCM IV hydration, calcitonin and IV bisphophonates or denosumab.B
Several medications, including bisphosphonates, calcitonin, and corticosteroids, may give temporary control of hypercalcemia of malignancy (see and ).B
Surgical excision of parathyroid adenoma is curative in greater than 95% of primary hyperparathyroidism cases.B
Surgical treatment of asymptomatic hyperparathyroidism is "curative" but does not improve quality of life.A
Surgical treatment of primary hyperparathyroidism does not appear to reduce mortality.

Rehydrate patient, followed by IV bisphosphonates or denosumab, particularly in hypercalcemia of malignancy (HCM). A typical initial hydration regimen (in a patient without heart failure) would be 300 to 500 mL/h of normal saline followed by 4 mg zoledronic acid or 60 mg pamidronate.

Addition of calcitonin for up to 48 to 72 hours is recommended for patients with severe HCM and serum calcium > 14 mg/dl (3.5 mmol/L). Denosumab is preferred over IV bisphosphonates for treatment of severe or symptomatic HCM.
Bisphosphonates (pamidronate, ibandronate, etidronate) help prevent fractures in patients with bony metastases and myeloma ().

Bisphosphonates in standard doses may be used to protect bone integrity in primary hyperparathyroidism if surgery is not elected. IV bisphosphonates can also reduce the calcium level with an onset of action of 2 to 4 days.
Calcitonin or corticosteroids can all be used to reduce severely elevated calcium levels, but their effect is short term ().

In a meta-analysis of 6 studies, there were no significant differences between intermittent intravenous and oral calcitriol in the treatment of secondary hyperparathyroidism in patients undergoing chronic hemodialysis.
Calcitonin is not effective in relieving the pain of bony metastases.

Denosumab therapy leading to a decrease in osteoclasts, may be effective in hypercalcemia of malignancy in patients not responding to bisphosphonates. In a small trial of 15 such patients, within 10 days of treatment 12 (80%) responded with a serum calcium level <11.5 mg/dL, and 10 had a complete response (serum calcium <10. 5 mg/dL).
The use of loop diuretics for hypercalcemia is not routinely encouraged given the unclear kalliuretic effect, potential for worsening volume depletion, and electrolyte derangements.
Glucocorticoids help inhibit vitamin D conversion to calcitriol and may be useful for patients with hypercalcemia due to granulomatous disease.
In a recent RCT, use of IV or IO calcium in patients with out-of-hospital cardiac arrest did not improve ROSC.

Surgery is suggested for patients with primary hyperparathyroidism who are symptomatic or asymptomatic patients with one or more of the following: serum calcium >1.0 mg/dL above upper limit of normal, 24-hour urinary calcium >250 mg/day in women or > 300 mg/day in men,, creatinine clearance reduced by 30% from normal for age, osteoporosis, age <50 years.
A randomized trial of 191 asymptomatic patients with serum calcium between 10.4 and 11.4 followed for 3 years found that surgery did not improve outcomes.
A recent trial showed that increased levels of calcium and/or parathyroid hormone after parathyroidectomy is associated with 2.7 to 4.3 times the risk of recurrent primary hyperparathyroidism.
Patients with primary hyperparathyroidism who do not receive surgery should maintain good hydration and avoid excessive calcium intake.
Radiation may be palliative for bony metastasis.
Vitamin D supplementation for greater than 24 weeks is assoicated with an increased risk of hypercalcemia (RR 1.54) and hypercalciuria (RR 1.64) compared to placebo.
Primary hyperparathyroidism with mild hypercalcemia is a benign disease and may not need any therapy.B

Hypercalcemia of malignancy signifies a poor prognosis. In one study, the presence of 1 or more of four poor-prognosis factors (liver metastasis, squamous cell carcinoma, hypoalbuminemia, and calcemia >2.83 mmol) predicted mortality; patients with a score of 0 had a median overall survival of 797 days while patients with a score of 1 or more had a median overall survival of 49 days.B
